lines.text: Ten factorial ends in two zeros. Twenty factorial ends in four. Twice as many!
lines.caption: Ten factorial ends in two zeros. Twenty factorial ends in four. Twice as many!

lines.text: But eight factorial ends in one zero, and sixteen factorial ends in THREE.
lines.caption: But eight factorial ends in one zero, and sixteen factorial ends in THREE.

lines.text: Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's find out exactly when doubling works.
lines.caption: Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's find out exactly when doubling works.

lines.text: Here's the question. n factorial means one times two times three, all the way up to n.
lines.caption: Here's the question. n factorial means one times two times three, all the way up to n.

lines.text: For how many whole numbers n, from one to one hundred, does this happen?
lines.caption: For how many whole numbers n, from one to one hundred, does this happen?

lines.text: The factorial of two n ends in exactly twice as many zeros as n factorial.
lines.caption: The factorial of two n ends in exactly twice as many zeros as n factorial.

lines.text: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.
lines.caption: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

lines.text: So we sort every n into two groups. Doubling works, or it doesn't.
lines.caption: So we sort every n into two groups. Doubling works, or it doesn't.

lines.text: Ten works. Eight doesn't, because three is more than twice one. We need a rule.
lines.caption: Ten works. Eight doesn't, because three is more than twice one. We need a rule.

lines.text: Our job: count how many numbers, from one to one hundred, land in the works group.
lines.caption: Our job: count how many numbers, from one to one hundred, land in the works group.

lines.text: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
lines.caption: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

lines.text: Welcome back! Each zero at the end is a factor of ten, and ten is two times five.
lines.caption: Welcome back! Each zero at the end is a factor of ten, and ten is two times five.

lines.text: A factorial has way more twos than fives. So we just count the fives.
lines.caption: A factorial has way more twos than fives. So we just count the fives.

lines.text: Every multiple of five gives one five. That's n over five, rounded down.
lines.caption: Every multiple of five gives one five. That's n over five, rounded down.

lines.text: Every multiple of twenty-five gives one extra five. That's n over twenty-five, rounded down.
lines.caption: Every multiple of twenty-five gives one extra five. That's n over twenty-five, rounded down.

lines.text: The factorial of two n goes up to two hundred. So it also gets a one hundred twenty-five term.
lines.caption: The factorial of two n goes up to two hundred. So it also gets a one hundred twenty-five term.

lines.text: Now the key question. Does doubling n double each rounded-down term?
lines.caption: Now the key question. Does doubling n double each rounded-down term?

lines.text: Eight over five is one, remainder three. Double it: sixteen over five is three. Not two, but THREE!
lines.caption: Eight over five is one, remainder three. Double it: sixteen over five is three. Not two, but THREE!

lines.text: The remainder three doubled to six. Six is at least five, so it spills one extra five.
lines.caption: The remainder three doubled to six. Six is at least five, so it spills one extra five.

lines.text: Now try seven. The remainder two doubles to four. No spill, so one becomes exactly two.
lines.caption: Now try seven. The remainder two doubles to four. No spill, so one becomes exactly two.

lines.text: So the fives term doubles exactly when the remainder is zero, one or two.
lines.caption: So the fives term doubles exactly when the remainder is zero, one or two.

lines.text: Same for twenty-five. That term doubles exactly when the remainder is twelve or less.
lines.caption: Same for twenty-five. That term doubles exactly when the remainder is twelve or less.

lines.text: A term never comes out short. So for exactly twice the zeros, no term may spill.
lines.caption: A term never comes out short. So for exactly twice the zeros, no term may spill.

lines.text: n factorial has no one hundred twenty-five term, so two n factorial can't have one either: two n is under one hundred twenty-five, so n is at most sixty-two.
lines.caption: n factorial has no one hundred twenty-five term, so two n factorial can't have one either: two n is under one hundred twenty-five, so n is at most sixty-two.

lines.text: Let's lay out the numbers in rows of twenty-five, and keep only the ones that pass.
lines.caption: Let's lay out the numbers in rows of twenty-five, and keep only the ones that pass.

lines.text: Rule one: the remainder by five is zero, one or two. Keep three columns out of every five.
lines.caption: Rule one: the remainder by five is zero, one or two. Keep three columns out of every five.

lines.text: Rule two: the remainder by twenty-five is twelve or less. Keep the left part of each row.
lines.caption: Rule two: the remainder by twenty-five is twelve or less. Keep the left part of each row.

lines.text: Rule three: n is at most sixty-two. Cross out everything after that.
lines.caption: Rule three: n is at most sixty-two. Cross out everything after that.

lines.text: One and two count too. Two factorial and four factorial have no zeros, and twice zero is zero.
lines.caption: One and two count too. Two factorial and four factorial have no zeros, and twice zero is zero.

lines.text: The first row keeps eight, since n starts at one. The next two rows keep nine each.
lines.caption: The first row keeps eight, since n starts at one. The next two rows keep nine each.

lines.text: Eight plus nine plus nine is <short pause> twenty-six! Choice C.
lines.caption: Eight plus nine plus nine is twenty-six! Choice C.

lines.text: Here's a faster way. Write n in base five, with ones, fives and twenty-fives.
lines.caption: Here's a faster way. Write n in base five, with ones, fives and twenty-fives.

lines.text: Thirty-seven is twenty-five, plus two fives, plus two ones. In base five, that's one, two, two.
lines.caption: Thirty-seven is twenty-five, plus two fives, plus two ones. In base five, that's one, two, two.

lines.text: Rule one says the ones digit is at most two.
lines.caption: Rule one says the ones digit is at most two.

lines.text: Rule two then says the fives digit is at most two. Three fives would already pass twelve.
lines.caption: Rule two then says the fives digit is at most two. Three fives would already pass twelve.

lines.text: And sixty-two in base five is two, two, two. So every digit is zero, one or two.
lines.caption: And sixty-two in base five is two, two, two. So every digit is zero, one or two.

lines.text: Three choices for each of three digits. Three times three times three is twenty-seven.
lines.caption: Three choices for each of three digits. Three times three times three is twenty-seven.

lines.text: Drop zero, zero, zero, since n starts at one. Twenty-six again!
lines.caption: Drop zero, zero, zero, since n starts at one. Twenty-six again!

lines.text: When would you pick this one? When doubling meets fives, think base five, with no carries.
lines.caption: When would you pick this one? When doubling meets fives, think base five, with no carries.

lines.text: Each wrong answer is a trap. Choice A, twenty, is what you'd get from the multiples of five.
lines.caption: Each wrong answer is a trap. Choice A, twenty, is what you'd get from the multiples of five.

lines.text: B, twenty-four, is what you'd get if you skipped one and two. But they count!
lines.caption: B, twenty-four, is what you'd get if you skipped one and two. But they count!

lines.text: D, thirty, is what you'd get if you used the last digit in base ten, ending in zero, one or two.
lines.caption: D, thirty, is what you'd get if you used the last digit in base ten, ending in zero, one or two.

lines.text: Choice E, fifty, is what you'd get if you thought doubling works half the time. The rules are stricter.
lines.caption: Choice E, fifty, is what you'd get if you thought doubling works half the time. The rules are stricter.

lines.text: So here's a great habit. When you double a rounded-down number, check the remainder.
lines.caption: So here's a great habit. When you double a rounded-down number, check the remainder.

lines.text: Your turn! For how many n from one to one hundred does three n factorial end in exactly three times as many zeros as n factorial?
lines.caption: Your turn! For how many n from one to one hundred does three n factorial end in exactly three times as many zeros as n factorial?

lines.text: Pause the video, and go for it!
lines.caption: Pause the video, and go for it!

lines.text: Three times the remainder must stay under five. So the remainder by five is zero or one.
lines.caption: Three times the remainder must stay under five. So the remainder by five is zero or one.

lines.text: By twenty-five, the remainder must be eight or less. Three times nine is too big.
lines.caption: By twenty-five, the remainder must be eight or less. Three times nine is too big.

lines.text: And three n must stay under one hundred twenty-five. So n is at most forty-one.
lines.caption: And three n must stay under one hundred twenty-five. So n is at most forty-one.

lines.text: Just like before, every base-five digit is zero or one. Two times two times two is eight.
lines.caption: Just like before, every base-five digit is zero or one. Two times two times two is eight.

lines.text: Drop the zero, and that's seven!
lines.caption: Drop the zero, and that's seven!

lines.text: The big idea: count the fives, as a sum of rounded-down terms.
lines.caption: The big idea: count the fives, as a sum of rounded-down terms.

lines.text: Doubling keeps a term exactly double when its remainder is less than half the divisor. No spills!
lines.caption: Doubling keeps a term exactly double when its remainder is less than half the divisor. No spills!
